name: Bio-Oil

card.summary: Popular scar and stretch mark oil with no product-specific evidence found here.
card.note: Sources for this product were thin.

quick.overview:
Bio-Oil is a branded cosmetic oil marketed for scars and stretch marks.
No product-specific trials exist; general references say creams and oils have not been shown to prevent stretch marks in pregnancy.
quick.mechanism: Moisturizing oils soften skin surface; no mechanism for changing scar or stretch mark structure has been established.
quick.risks: No safety data have been found. As a cosmetic, it is not subject to drug approval.

lead: Bio-Oil is a branded skincare oil that people apply to the skin to make scars, stretch marks and uneven skin tone look smoother and more even. It is sold over the counter as a cosmetic and used as a daily routine: the oil is massaged into the area of concern, which keeps the skin soft and supple while marks mature and fade.[2] Its maker describes it as suitable for scars, stretch marks, uneven skin tone, ageing skin and dehydrated skin.[2]

The product was created in South Africa by cosmetic chemist Dieter Beier and launched in 1987, first as a dry-skin product, and was repositioned for scars and stretch marks after the Letschert brothers bought its parent company Union Swiss in 2000.[3][4] It then spread to the United Kingdom in 2002 and to dozens of other markets, becoming a drugstore staple.[3][4] A 2016 survey of 753 pregnant women in Ireland found that Bio-Oil was the most commonly used product for preventing or reducing stretch marks, used by about 61 percent of respondents who used a product.[6]

Stretch marks (striae) appear in areas of stored fat such as the abdomen, thighs, hips and breasts, most often during pregnancy, puberty, weight gain or muscle gain.[1] That makes the oil a talking point for people who bulk, gain muscle quickly or lose weight, as well as for people with surgical or acne scars. The manufacturer cites its own sponsored studies; independent reviews of topical products for stretch marks describe a limited number of studies overall.[2][7]

chain: Oil is massaged into scars or stretch marks
Marks look smoother and less conspicuous as they fade
angle.text: Users apply the oil to the abdomen, hips, thighs, arms or scars with the goal of softer, more even-looking skin. The benefit people describe is cosmetic: a moisturised surface that makes marks less noticeable while they mature.

infobox: Scars, stretch marks, uneven skin tone, ageing and dehydrated skin [2]
Union Swiss; owned by David and Justin Letschert since 2000 [4]

paras: The product is positioned for three appearance goals: fading the look of scars, softening the look of stretch marks, and improving uneven skin tone.[2] Wikipedia notes that stretch marks are most often seen on the abdomen, breasts, thighs, hips and buttocks and affect young women the most; about 90 percent of pregnant women are affected, with higher risk in teenagers and with large weight gain.[1]
Other triggers listed include rapid growth, weight gain, muscle gain and corticosteroid use, which is why people who build muscle or change weight quickly sometimes reach for a body oil.[1]

The manufacturer's product information says to massage the oil into cleansed skin twice daily, for at least three months for scars and stretch marks. It advises against using it on open wounds or broken skin, to avoid the eyes and mucous membranes, and to use sunscreen because the oil gives no UV protection. It lists 23 fragrance allergens, recommends a patch test, and suggests that people who are pregnant or taking medicines speak to a doctor before use.[2]

According to the manufacturer, the formula uses oil as a base to carry vitamins and plant-derived ingredients, together with PurCellin Oil, a proprietary additive that gives a lighter, thinner feel.[2][3] The company states that the vitamin A content is well below EU limits for body lotions.[2] Refinery29 reports that Beier was inspired by the preen-gland oil of ducks while researching oil-based skincare.[3]

Beier began researching oil-based skincare in the early 1970s, and Bio-Oil launched in South Africa in 1987 as a dry-skin product.[3] Union Swiss itself had been importing Swiss skincare products since 1954.[4] In 2000 brothers David and Justin Letschert, previously mergers-and-acquisitions advisers, bought Union Swiss, sold off most of its roughly 120 other products and focused on Bio-Oil, repositioning it for scars and stretch marks and relying on consumer testimonials rather than traditional advertising.[4]

Bizcommunity reports that for the 2002 UK launch Boots initially refused to stock it unless the word 'scars' was removed from the packaging, and that Japanese rules banning the word shaped the brand's marketing there; within three years it was the top-selling body-care product in the UK.[4] Refinery29 (2019) described it as a 'cult favorite' sold in 125 countries, with celebrity endorsements, and a CVS bestseller in 2018.[3]

On its product-information pages the manufacturer describes studies run by the proDERM institute in Hamburg. A scar study of 36 women reported improvement in 66 percent of subjects at 2 weeks and 92 percent at 8 weeks; a stretch-mark study of 38 women reported improvement in 95 percent at 2 weeks and 100 percent at 8 weeks. Other company-described work covers acne scars in 44 Chinese subjects over 10 weeks, uneven skin tone and ageing skin in 67 women over 12 weeks, and laboratory hydration measurements.[2] The company states that results vary between individuals.[2] The Irish News repeated a company claim of a 2010 placebo-controlled trial in which 93 percent of users saw scars improve over eight weeks.[5]

Wikipedia reports that a Cochrane review (Brennan and colleagues, 2012) did not find evidence that creams and oils prevent or reduce stretch marks in pregnancy, and that tretinoin, hyaluronic acid and lasers are among other approaches tried.[1] A 2016 review of topicals for striae found few studies (11) of topical efficacy, reported level-2 evidence for two creams and no effect for cocoa butter and olive oil, and called for randomised trials.[7] A 2019 review likewise describes a paucity of strong evidence for stretch-mark treatments, listing topical tretinoin, glycolic acid, lasers and other procedures as commonly cited options.[8]

The authors of the 2016 Irish survey concluded that high-quality evidence on the effectiveness of Bio-Oil and other products is needed.[6] Consultant dermatologist Ophelia Veraitch told the Irish News that scars take about 18 months to remodel, that daily massage in that period helps smooth irregularities, and that there is 'little evidence that it's more effective than Vaseline'.[5]

Published human data on the branded product consist mainly of the manufacturer-sponsored studies described above.[2] Independent literature includes a 2016 survey documenting its popularity among pregnant women and reviews of topical stretch-mark products that call for randomised trials.[6][7] Searches of the biomedical literature for 'bio-oil' mainly return work on biofuel, which is unrelated.

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation, lifters mention Bio-Oil in connection with stretch marks from bulking and growing muscle. One poster in a long training thread says they are using it and also increasing fat intake during their next bulk, another recommends it as a product specifically for scars and stretch marks, and a third jokes about needing some for growing legs.[9][10][11]
Bio-Oil is regulated as a cosmetic and is not subject to drug approval. Its label lists fragrance allergens and advises a patch test.[2]

timeline.event: Union Swiss begins importing Swiss skincare products into South Africa. [4]
Chemist Dieter Beier starts researching oil-based skincare. [3]
Bio-Oil launches in South Africa as a dry-skin product. [3][4]
David and Justin Letschert buy Union Swiss and focus on Bio-Oil, repositioning it for scars and stretch marks. [4]
UK launch; Boots initially asks for the word 'scars' to be removed from the pack. [4]
Cochrane review (Brennan et al.) finds no evidence that creams and oils prevent or reduce stretch marks in pregnancy. [1]
Irish survey of 753 pregnant women finds Bio-Oil the most commonly used anti-stretch-mark product. [6]

lore.intro: Bio-Oil is discussed in appearance and fitness communities as a familiar over-the-counter option for stretch marks from bulking and for scars.[9][10]

claims.claim: Bio-Oil fades scars and stretch marks
claims.believers: Users and the maker's sponsored studies report visible improvement over weeks of daily massage; testimonials drove its repositioning.[2][4]
claims.experts: The manufacturer's trials are company-sponsored; independent reviews report limited trial data on topicals for stretch marks and no product shown to be most effective.[2][7]

claims.claim: Applying oil during a bulk helps prevent stretch marks
claims.believers: Lifters on T Nation mention using it while bulking and growing muscle.[9][11]
claims.experts: The Cochrane review summarised on Wikipedia did not find evidence that creams and oils prevent stretch marks in pregnancy; no trial in muscle gain was found.[1]

claims.claim: Massage rather than the oil does the work
claims.believers: Proponents of massage say daily rubbing while a scar remodels helps smooth irregularities, and that the oil makes massage easier.[5]
claims.experts: Dermatologist Ophelia Veraitch told the Irish News that the oil may make massage easier but that there is little evidence it beats Vaseline.[5]

claims.claim: The oil improves uneven skin tone and ageing skin
claims.believers: The company reports 12-week studies in 67 women with improvements in tone.[2]
claims.experts: No independent published trial has tested this.
